title: To Build a Fire
focus: human limits in an indifferent nature

teacherSummary.text: A newcomer to the Yukon sets out alone with a wolf-dog at seventy-five below zero, ignoring an old-timer's warning never to travel alone in such cold. He breaks through ice and wets his feet, builds a fire under a snow-laden spruce, and the snow falls and puts it out. His hands freeze; he fails to light another, thinks of killing the dog for warmth, runs in panic, and freezes to death. The dog trots off toward camp.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “To Build a Fire,” how does London show human limits in an indifferent nature? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the setting you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In To Build a Fire, how does London develop the idea of human limits in an indifferent nature? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the setting in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how To Build a Fire develops the idea of human limits in an indifferent nature. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of setting and conflict shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of To Build a Fire (where it begins, turns and ends) and its setting shape the reader's understanding of human limits in an indifferent nature. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what To Build a Fire suggests about human limits in an indifferent nature. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's setting and conflict), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jack London uses setting in To Build a Fire to complicate the reader's understanding of human limits in an indifferent nature. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate To Build a Fire within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of human limits in an indifferent nature responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read To Build a Fire alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of human limits in an indifferent nature follows or bends those conventions, using the setting as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to To Build a Fire and its treatment of human limits in an indifferent nature. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's setting and conflict, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads To Build a Fire as evidence for a larger claim about human limits in an indifferent nature in To Build a Fire. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads To Build a Fire as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of human limits in an indifferent nature. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on To Build a Fire.

satQuestions.passage: Day had broken cold and gray, exceedingly cold and gray, when the man turned aside from the main Yukon trail and climbed the high earth-bank, where a dim and little-travelled trail led eastward through the fat spruce timberland. It was a steep bank, and he paused for breath at the top, excusing the act to himself by looking at his watch. It was nine o'clock. There was no sun nor hint of sun, though there was not a cloud in the sky. It was a clear day, and yet there seemed an intangible pall over the face of things, a subtle gloom that made the day dark, and that was due to the absence of sun. This fact did not worry the man. He was used to the lack of sun. It had been days since he had seen the sun, and he knew that a few more days must pass before that cheerful orb, due south, would just peep above the sky-line and dip immediately from view.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “To Build a Fire”?
options: Hope created by an act of sacrifice
Human limits in an indifferent nature
The mind's final escape at the moment of death

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: When have you ignored good advice? What happened? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Heads-up: this story includes death by freezing.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are avalanche, numbness, advertised, exhaled, protruding. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “It grew like an avalanche, and it descended without warning upon the man and the fire, and the fire was blotted out!” In this sentence it means: a slide of large masses of snow and ice and mud down a mountain. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of To Build a Fire would have known. London went to the Klondike in 1897. This 1908 version (The Century) replaced a 1902 version for boys in which the man survives. Why does this story matter? A central example of literary naturalism. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for setting.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Day had broken cold and gray, exceedingly cold and gray, when the man turned aside from the main Yukon trail and climbed the high earth-bank, where a dim and little-travelled trail led eastward through the fat spruce tim” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to human limits in an indifferent nature? When I find setting, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for setting.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of setting. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Day had broken cold and gray, exceedingly cold and gray, when the man turned aside from the main Yukon trail and climbed the high earth-bank, where a dim and little-travelled trail led eastward through the fat spruce timberland. It was a steep bank, and he paused for breath at the top, excusing the act to himself by looking at his watch. It was nine o'clock. There was no sun nor hint of sun, though there was not a cloud in the sky. It was a clear day, and yet there seemed an intangible pall over the face of things, a subtle gloom that made the day dark, and that was due to the absence of sun. This fact did not worry the man. segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to nature's indifference? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about human limits in an indifferent nature, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
